newsitem.title: UK: Mark tone firm, Buba rate policy speculation buoys.
newsitem.headline: Mark tone firm, Buba rate policy speculation buoys.

text.p: The mark was firmer on most European crosses, its sentiment boosted by continued speculation that the Bundesbank may alter its money market policy to allow German rates to head higher.

Such expectations had emerged late last week when the Bundesbank council, before a four-week break, fixed its key repo rate for the next two weeks at 3.00 percent but left undecided the rate for the remaining two.

"It would certainly be a really big thing for the mark if that (a change in money market policy) were to happen and so it's supporting the mark against most other currencies even now," said one trader at a Japanese bank here.
"But at the moment there is still doubt as to whether the Bundesbank will do such a thing at this stage for the sake of the currency rate alone."

Speculation about a possible switch to a variable repo rate was heightened today by a comment by Buba council member Hans-Juergen Koebnick that at last week's meeting, the central bank had made provisions for a possible rate signal if necessary.
Koebnick, in an interview with German daily Handelsblatt, said the Bundesbank was considering conducting fixed and variable repo tenders at the same time.
Setting a floating repo rate would allow a natural, tighter monetary policy without a drastic change like a hike in the key discount or Lombard rates, analysts said.

"It may only result in a change of five basis points, but it would be enough to alert the market that they (the Bundesbank) are not happy with the situation," said Adrian Davies, senior strategist at Societe Generale Strauss Turnbull.

The Bundesbank could defend such a move by arguing that it was not just an attempt to shore up the ailing mark but also a way of pre-empting imported inflation resulting from the mark's decline, said Francis Breedon, foreign exchange analyst at Lehman Brothers.
Higher rates in Germany may in fact be welcomed by European nations in the process of aligning their interest rates with Germany's ahead of European monetary union, analysts said.
Many of the EMU candidate economies are performing better than Germany's, they said, and so would appreciate higher rates.
"The only ones who would be disturbed by it are the French...and in that case the Germans could argue that it was all necessary for the credibility of the euro," Breedon said.
The mark had slipped to near its session lows on the European crosses by midday after trading with a firm tone most of the morning.
It was at 3.3705/09 French francs at 1055 GMT against 3.3710/15 in late European trade on Tuesday, and at 975.05/35 lire against 975.50/70.

Traders noted the mark was doing well against the Swiss franc and Swedish crown today, adding that these had been the currencies that had recently gained on the mark on the perception that they were safe havens outside the EMU bloc.
Mark/Swiss was at 82.74/80 after rising to 82.86 earlier, against Tuesday's 82.66/69. Mark/Swedish was at 4.3330/60, off its morning high of 4.3405 but up from yesterday's 4.3300/30.
The guilder bucked the trend, ticking up against the mark after falling to its lowest in nearly four years on Tuesday.

Speculation that the Dutch central bank may raise its key special advances money market rate on Thursday, which emerged when the guilder fell below its ERM central rate of 1.12673 to the mark Tuesday, was still continuing.
The guilder had recovered above its ERM central rate early on Wednesday, and was quoted at its session high of 1.126050/6150 against 1.126900/7000 late on Tuesday.
-- Chizu Nomiyama, London Forex Desk, +44-171-542-6721
